701.title: The Didache
701.hook: an early manual: two ways, baptism in running water, fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays
701.howItsDone: Catholics today keep Friday as a day of penance, some fast or abstain in small ways during the week, and the Didache is read by students of the early Church as a window into its first practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ichthys, the fish whose letters spell a creed. Your line was the secret sign.

A brand-new church needs a handbook. What goes in it? How to live. How to baptize. When to fast, and how often to pray. What to do about a traveling preacher who shows up and won't leave. An early Christian handbook covers all of it in a few short pages. On that last problem it's wonderfully practical: let the visiting apostle stay a day, two if he needs it. If he stays three, he's a false prophet. If he asks for money, same verdict. Its name is the Didache.
screen: `A HANDBOOK FOR A NEW CHURCH.` → `LIVE, BAPTIZE, FAST, PRAY.` → `THREE DAYS? FALSE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Didache is Greek for teaching. The book isn't in the Bible, but it gives a close look at how some early Christians lived. First, a fork in the road. In Lightfoot's translation: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways." The way of life: love the God who made you, love your neighbor as yourself, and don't do to another what you wouldn't want done to you. That's the again in today's line, because the picture is older. In Deuteronomy, Moses sets life and death before the people and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Choose therefore life." Jesus speaks of a narrow gate and a wide one. The Didache hands the same choice to a new community. Second, baptism: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in running water, living water. If there isn't any, use other water, cold if you can, warm if you must. If there's not enough for that, pour water on the head three times, in that same threefold name. Strict about the meaning, generous about the river. Third, fasting and prayer. Christians fast on Wednesday and Friday, it says, and pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. Catholics still keep Friday as a day of penance. Fourth, the bread. The Didache gives thanksgiving prayers for the cup and the broken bread, and one pictures the bread as grain once scattered over the mountains and gathered into one loaf, the way the Church is gathered from the ends of the earth. A handbook about water, food and visitors, and underneath it all, two roads and a choice made again every day.
screen: `TWO WAYS: LIFE AND DEATH.` · `LIVING WATER, OR WHATEVER WATER.` · `WEDNESDAY, FRIDAY, THREE PRAYERS.` · `SCATTERED GRAIN, ONE LOAF.` · then, large: `CHOOSE THEREFORE LIFE.`

segments.voice: If fasting is safe for you, choose one small thing to go without on Wednesday, the Didache's fast day: a snack, a second coffee, an hour of scrolling. Decide now what that little hunger will remind you of: a person, a prayer, the two ways. If you pray, offer the day ahead.

702.title: Clement writes to Corinth (c. 96)
702.hook: the bishop of Rome writes to calm a quarrelling church
702.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Clement of Rome as an early pope and, by tradition, a martyr, and his name is among the saints remembered in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Didache: two ways, living water, Wednesday and Friday fasts. Your line was two ways, again.

The letter opens with an apology for being late. The church at Rome has been hit by sudden troubles, one after another, and only now can it turn to the news from Corinth. The news is bad. A few headstrong people there have pushed out leaders who had served the church well, and the community is split. Word of the fight has traveled far enough that outsiders are talking. So Rome writes a long letter to a church across the sea, with one aim: peace.
screen: `SORRY THIS IS LATE.` → `CORINTH HAS SPLIT.` → `ROME WRITES FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, who's writing. The letter comes from the church of God staying at Rome, to the church of God staying at Corinth. It never signs a name. An early tradition gives it to Clement, whom Catholics count among the early bishops of Rome after Peter. Second, how he argues: not with threats, but with stories. Jealousy, he says, has done damage since Cain and Abel, and in their own generation it struck down the greatest pillars of the Church, Peter and Paul. Third, a clever move. Corinth had quarreled before. Pick up the letter of the blessed apostle Paul, Clement says, and read it again. Paul had written to them about the same sickness: one says I belong to Paul, another to Apollos, another to Cephas. You took sides then, Clement says, and that was less shameful, because at least you were choosing among apostles and a man they trusted. Now you've thrown out good leaders because of a few people. Fourth, the cure. Who among you is noble, or tender-hearted, or full of love? Let that person say: if this split is because of me, I'll go away, wherever you like, and do what the people want, only let the flock of Christ be at peace. Peace, here, isn't winning. It's being willing to step aside. He sends trusted messengers with the letter, and asks them to come back soon with news of peace. Catholics have long read the letter as an early sign of the Roman church caring for the others. Other readers see one sister church helping another. Both can see a church that loved peace enough to write.

segments.voice: Think of a disagreement near you, in your family, your parish, your group chat, and draft three sentences in your head the way Clement might. Own something first, an apology or a fault; remind them of something good you share; then say what you're willing to give up. Don't send it; let it sit in you, and if you pray, ask peace for the people in it.

703.title: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107)
703.hook: on his way to the lions he writes seven letters, the first to use the words the catholic church
703.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Ignatius of Antioch each year, name him in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and his letters appear in the Office of Readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement writes to Corinth: a letter for peace, and the noble one willing to step aside. Your line was peace in the church.

A prisoner is being marched across Asia toward Rome. He's chained to a squad of soldiers, and in one letter he calls them ten leopards, who only get worse the kinder he is to them. At the end of the road, wild beasts wait in the arena. Along the way, churches send people to meet him, sit with him, bring news. And whenever he can, the prisoner writes letters back. He's the bishop of Antioch, and his name is Ignatius.
screen: `A PRISONER ON THE ROAD TO ROME.` → `TEN LEOPARDS.` → `LETTERS FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, where he comes from. Antioch is the city where, Acts says, the disciples were first called Christians. Ignatius leads that church as its bishop. In his letters' greetings he gives himself a second name: Theophorus, God-bearer. Second, the letter to Rome. The Christians there might have had friends with influence, people who could get a sentence changed. Ignatius begs them not to try. Don't be kind to me at the wrong time, he says; let me reach God. Then the line today's carry comes from: I am God's wheat, ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. A bishop who has broken the bread of the Eucharist for his people now pictures his own body as grain for that bread. Third, a word still on church signs. To the Christians of Smyrna he writes: stay with your bishop, and just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church. Catholic is a Greek word meaning universal, whole. Ignatius uses it for the whole Church, gathered around Christ, wherever it is. Fourth, what worried him most. Some teachers said Jesus only seemed to have a body, only seemed to suffer. Ignatius pushes back again and again: Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly suffered and truly rose. For a man about to suffer in his own body, that mattered. His story is kept as a martyr's, not as a call to go looking for death, but as a picture of a life given away so completely that even its ending could become bread for others.
screen: `ANTIOCH, THEOPHORUS.` · `DON'T RESCUE ME.` · `WHERE CHRIST IS, THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.` · `TRULY BORN, TRULY SUFFERED.` · then, large: `I AM GOD'S WHEAT.`

segments.voice: Say his line to yourself on an out-breath: I am God's wheat. Then ask what is being ground in your life right now, a hard job, a long illness, a slow grief, and, without having to like it, what bread it might become, for you or someone else. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, let the picture of wheat and bread rest in you.

704.title: The medicine of immortality
704.hook: Ignatius calls the Eucharist the medicine of immortality and stresses unity with the bishop
704.howItsDone: At every Catholic Mass the local bishop is named in the Eucharistic Prayer, and Catholics receive Communion as the body and blood of Christ, in communion with their bishop and the pope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophorus: Ignatius, the God-bearer, writing on his road to the beasts. Your line was wheat of God.

A bathroom cabinet is a small pharmacy: something for headaches, something for a cough, a half-finished prescription. Medicine is an ordinary thing to keep in a house. It's also an admission: bodies break, and everyone would like to put off the end a little longer. Ignatius, still on his road to Rome, reaches for exactly that ordinary word when he writes about the bread Christians share.
screen: `A CABINET OF MEDICINES.` → `BODIES BREAK.` → `IGNATIUS REACHES FOR THAT WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Writing to the Christians of Ephesus, Ignatius asks them to gather in one faith around their bishop and priests, breaking one bread, which he calls "the medicine of immortality": an antidote, he adds, so that we should not die but live forever in Jesus Christ. In Greek, pharmakon athanasias. The cure for death, handed out at a table. Second, where the picture comes from. In John's Gospel Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Whoever eats this bread, he goes on, will live forever. Ignatius gives that hope a household name: medicine. Third, why the bishop comes into it. For Ignatius, the cure works in a body that holds together. To Philadelphia he writes: take care to keep one Eucharist, for there is one flesh of our Lord, one cup, one altar, as there is one bishop. To Smyrna he says the Eucharist should be the one celebrated with the bishop, or someone he appoints. Earlier in the letter to Ephesus, he calls Christ the one physician. Fourth, how it's read today. Catholics, and Orthodox Christians too, read Ignatius as an early witness to what they believe: that the Eucharist is truly the body and blood of Christ, celebrated in communion with the bishop. In the letter to Smyrna he mentions people who stayed away from the Eucharist because they did not confess it to be the flesh of Christ. Some Protestant readers treasure his letters while reading these lines in their own way. At every Catholic Mass, the local bishop is still named aloud in the Eucharistic Prayer, right in the middle of the bread and the cup. One bread, one bishop, said at once.
screen: `PHARMAKON ATHANASIAS.` · `THE LIVING BREAD.` · `ONE CUP, ONE ALTAR, ONE BISHOP.` · `NAMED AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THE MEDICINE OF IMMORTALITY.`

segments.voice: If you're Catholic and know your bishop's name, hold it in mind, or listen for it in the Eucharistic Prayer next time you're at Mass; on another path, think of whoever holds your community together, a pastor, a principal, a parent. Picture them on a hard day, with everyone's complaints on their desk. If you pray, ask wisdom and strength for them; if you don't, wish them well, plainly.

705.title: Polycarp (c. 155)
705.hook: the old bishop refuses to curse Christ: eighty-six years I have served him
705.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Polycarp each year, and the Church's calendar often sets a saint's day on the day of death, called the birth into heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pharmakon athanasias, Ignatius's medicine of immortality, kept with the bishop. Your line was one bread, one bishop.

Swear the oath, curse Christ, and I'll let you go. A Roman governor says it in a packed stadium in Smyrna, to a very old man. The crowd is shouting. The governor presses again and again, and threatens wild beasts, then fire. The old man is Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna. Ignatius once wrote him a letter on the road to Rome. His answer to the governor is not an argument. It's a number.
screen: `A STADIUM IN SMYRNA.` → `REVILE THE CHRIST.` → `AN OLD MAN ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: His answer, in Lightfoot's translation of the Martyrdom of Polycarp: "Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" Eighty-six years: a life added up. First, the source: a letter from the church of Smyrna to another church, telling what happened to their bishop. Second, the arrest. When soldiers find him at a farm outside the city, he comes down and talks with them. He has food and drink set out for them, as much as they want, and asks only for an hour to pray. He prays standing, remembering everyone he has ever met, small and great, for two hours, until some of the soldiers are sorry they came. Third, the stadium. As he walks in, the account says, a voice comes from heaven: be strong, Polycarp, and play the man. The governor tells him to respect his age, and to say: away with the atheists. That's what the crowd called Christians, because they wouldn't worship the gods. Polycarp looks at the crowd, waves his hand toward them, sighs, looks up to heaven, and says it: away with the atheists. He just means a different crowd. Fourth, what his church did next. They gathered his bones, more precious than jewels, they said, and planned to meet there to keep what they called the birthday of his martyrdom. The Catholic calendar still marks many saints on the day they died, which it calls their birth into heaven. Polycarp's church turned a death day into a birthday.

segments.voice: Say your age to yourself, then let the years go by in chunks: childhood, school, the first job, the move, the loss, the person who changed things. Don't stop to judge any of it; Polycarp didn't say every year was easy, only that the One he served had done him no wrong. If you pray, give thanks one stretch at a time; if you don't, notice that you're still here, and what carried you.

706.title: The letter to Diognetus
706.hook: Christians live in every country, as the soul lives in the body
706.howItsDone: Catholic teaching describes the calling of lay people as living the faith inside ordinary work, family and civic life, and the Second Vatican Council quoted the letter to Diognetus to say so.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polycarp, the old bishop in the stadium at Smyrna who would not curse Christ. Your line was eighty-six years.

A man named Diognetus has questions about the Christians. Who is this God they trust? Why do they look down on death, and refuse the gods of the Greeks? What is this love they have for one another? And why did this new way of living show up now, and not long ago? Someone writes him an answer. Nobody knows who wrote it, or who Diognetus was. The letter has no signature and no date. But its description of Christians would one day be quoted by a council of the Church.
screen: `DIOGNETUS HAS QUESTIONS.` → `NO SIGNATURE, NO DATE.` → `AN ANSWER THAT LASTED.`

segments.voice: First, the writer says, Christians look ordinary. They aren't marked off by country, language or customs. They don't live in cities of their own, or speak some odd dialect. They follow the local ways in clothes and food and daily life. Second, the paradox. They live in their own countries, but as visitors. Every foreign country is a homeland to them, and every homeland is foreign. They marry and have children like everyone else, but they don't abandon their babies. They share their table. They obey the laws, and in their own lives go further than the laws ask. They love all people, the letter says, and all people persecute them. Third, the picture behind today's line. In Lightfoot's translation: "In a word, what the soul is in a body, this the Christians are in the world." The soul is spread through every part of the body; Christians through the cities of the world. The soul lives in the body but isn't of the body; Christians live in the world but aren't of the world. The soul is unseen, but it holds the body together, and the writer says Christians hold the world together in the same quiet way. Fourth, why Catholics still read it. The Second Vatican Council borrowed the line for the calling of lay Catholics: what the soul is in the body, let Christians be in the world. Not a separate town. Not a fortress. Ordinary streets, ordinary jobs, ordinary food, and something inside that keeps the whole thing alive. It's a big claim, and the letter makes it calmly, as a description, to a stranger who simply asked.
screen: `ORDINARY ON THE OUTSIDE.` · `EVERY HOMELAND FOREIGN.` · `SPREAD THROUGH THE WHOLE BODY.` · `THE COUNCIL BORROWED IT.` · then, large: `WHAT THE SOUL IS IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who live or work nearest you, known by name or only by a nod, and let one of them come forward. What would make their week a little lighter: taking in a package, a note, an offer to help, something small enough that nobody needs to know? If you pray, hold that neighbor before God.

707.title: Justin describes the Mass (c. 155)
707.hook: a philosopher writes to the emperor about Sunday: readings, prayers, bread and wine, a collection for the poor
707.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics hear readings and a homily (the Liturgy of the Word), then the gifts are brought forward and the Eucharistic prayer ends in the great Amen before communion (the Liturgy of the Eucharist); parishes usually take a collection as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Diognetus: Christians as the soul in the body. Your line was the soul of the world.

The letter is addressed to the emperor of Rome, and the man writing it wears a philosopher's cloak. His name is Justin. He looked for the truth among the philosophers, one school after another, found Christ, and kept the cloak. Rumors about Christians are going around: secret meetings, strange meals, who knows what behind closed doors. Justin could simply ask for mercy. He does something bolder. He tells the emperor exactly what Christians do on Sunday, step by step.
screen: `A PHILOSOPHER'S CLOAK.` → `RUMORS ABOUT SUNDAY.` → `HE TELLS THE EMPEROR EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Justin is called an apologist. That doesn't mean he said sorry. In the Greek of the first letter of Peter, the answer Christians should be ready to give is an apologia, a defense. The Douay-Rheims puts it: ready to give "a reason of that hope which is in you." An apologist gives that reason to people outside. Justin's reason is a plain description. On the day called Sunday, he writes, people from the city and the countryside gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles, his name for the Gospels, or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time allows. Then the one presiding speaks, urging everyone to imitate these good things. All stand and pray. Bread is brought, and wine mixed with water. The presider offers prayers and thanksgiving, and the people answer: Amen. The deacons give each person a share, and carry some to those who are absent. Then the collection: those who have plenty, and are willing, give what each thinks fit. The presider uses it for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers passing through. Justin even explains the day: Sunday is when God began making the world, and when Jesus rose from the dead. And Christians, he says, don't receive this food as common bread and common drink. They call it the Eucharist. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this passage at length. It dates it around the year 155, and says the basic lines of the celebration have stayed the same until our own day: readings, a homily, prayers, the gifts, the great Amen, communion.
screen: `APOLOGIA: A DEFENSE.` · `SUNDAY: READINGS, PREACHING, PRAYERS.` · `BREAD, WINE AND WATER, THEN AMEN.` · `A COLLECTION FOR THE POOR.` · then, large: `THE SAME SHAPE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the last Mass you were at, or one you've seen: the readings, the preaching, everyone standing to pray, bread and wine carried forward, the Amen, communion, the basket going down the row. Lay Justin's Sunday over it and notice where they line up; if you've never been, hold the picture of a room of ordinary people doing these few things together. If you pray, say one quiet Amen.
Apologist. Someone who gives a defense of the faith, a reason, to people outside it, the way Justin did. Today's word.
Your line: the same Mass. From the Didache to Justin, the first Christians, in their own words. See you tomorrow.
